name: Exilis Ultra / Exilis Elite

lead: Exilis is a BTL radiofrequency machine used in clinics for non-surgical skin tightening and body contouring. Ultra and Elite are newer versions of the platform.
The sources reviewed describe the RF category in general; model-specific trial data were not found.

paras: Radiofrequency current is converted to heat in the skin, with the aim of contracting collagen and prompting new collagen over months.
Category reports include redness, swelling, pain, burns, blistering, pigment change and, less commonly, scarring or fat loss. Pacemakers and pregnancy are listed contraindications.

web.title: Radio-frequency skin tightening (Wikipedia, via Thermage redirect)

lead: Exilis is a radiofrequency (RF) skin-tightening device line made by BTL, listed on Wikipedia among commercial RF devices for non-surgical skin tightening [1]. Exilis Ultra and Exilis Elite are later versions of the platform, which is used by clinicians on the face and body.

RF skin tightening in general uses radiofrequency current converted to heat in tissue, with the aim of stimulating collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid and reducing lax skin and fine lines [1][2]. Wikipedia describes RF devices as an alternative to facelifts and other surgery and notes uses on jowls, abdomen, thighs and arms, as well as cellulite and body contouring [1].
Published sources available for this article describe the device category rather than Exilis specifically, so detail on model-specific specifications, trial results and pricing is limited.

paras: Wikipedia names Exilis as BTL's entry in the list of RF skin-tightening devices, alongside systems from Solta, Venus Concept, Syneron, Lutronic, Lumenis and DEKA [1]. RF devices heat the dermis to induce remodelling; Wikipedia cites an ideal dermal target temperature of 67 degrees C and notes that cooling can be manipulated to heat and reduce fat as well [1].

Grokipedia summarises category-wide reports of modest immediate tightening that increases over three to six months, and notes that many RF studies are small and lack randomized controls [2]. Wikipedia reports pain requiring sedation in some patients, skin dents from uneven healing, and fat necrosis or atrophic scarring with RF devices [1]. Grokipedia lists redness, swelling, burns, blistering and hyperpigmentation among reported effects, and pacemakers and pregnancy as contraindications [2].
